summary: Pre-Congestion Notification marks packets when traffic exceeds configured rates. This RFC defines how to encode three PCN states in the IP header using a single Diffserv codepoint, together with ECN bits.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network is close to running out of capacity, it can mark the packets that are using more than their share, so the edge of the network can act before anyone else notices. This RFC says how to write those marks into the IP header, using the two bits that normally carry congestion signalling plus one traffic class code.

questions: how are three pcn states encoded in the ip header
pcn encoding with a single dscp
what is threshold marking vs excess traffic marking
subtitle: How three levels of pre-congestion warning ride in the two congestion bits of an IP header beside one traffic class code.

tldr.problem: Pre-Congestion Notification lets a network meter traffic and warn the edges before the network is truly congested. Networks that use the controlled load behaviour need three marking states, but the earlier encoding defined in RFC 5696 could only carry two.
tldr.mechanism: The encoding reuses the two-bit Explicit Congestion Notification field of the IP header, in combination with a chosen Diffserv codepoint, to carry three PCN marking states: not-marked, threshold-marked and excess-traffic-marked. A fourth value of the same two bits marks packets that are not part of a PCN flow at all.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6660 is a Proposed Standard from July 2012 that obsoletes RFC 5696, whose encoding provided only a subset of the same capabilities. The document also states the rules for how ingress, interior and egress nodes must treat each marking.

today: RFC 6660 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012. It obsoletes RFC 5696, whose encoding provided only a subset of the same capabilities, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The objective of Pre-Congestion Notification, described in RFC 5559, is to protect the quality of service of inelastic flows within a Diffserv domain in a simple, scalable and robust fashion. Two mechanisms are used: admission control, which decides whether to admit or block a new flow request, and flow termination, which terminates some existing flows during serious pre-congestion. To achieve this, the overall rate of PCN traffic is metered on every link in the domain, and PCN packets are appropriately marked when certain configured rates are exceeded. Those configured rates are below the rate of the link, so the boundary nodes learn about overloads before any real congestion occurs, which is where the name pre-congestion notification comes from.

RFC 5670 provides two metering and marking functions that are generally configured with different reference rates. Threshold-marking marks all PCN packets once their traffic rate on a link exceeds the configured reference rate, the PCN-threshold-rate. Excess-traffic-marking marks only those PCN packets that exceed the configured reference rate, the PCN-excess-rate, which is typically larger than the threshold rate. Egress nodes monitor the marks of received PCN packets and pass information about them to Decision Points, which then decide whether to admit new flows or terminate existing flows.

The encoding of RFC 5696 described how two PCN marking states, not-marked and PCN-marked, could be encoded into the IP header using a single Diffserv codepoint, defining 01 as an experimental codepoint with guidelines for its use. Two marking states are sufficient for the Single Marking edge behaviour, but PCN domains using the controlled load edge behaviour require three marking states. This document extends the earlier encoding by redefining the experimental codepoint as a third PCN marking state in the IP header, while still using a single Diffserv codepoint, and the scheme is therefore called the 3-in-1 PCN encoding. It obsoletes the encoding of RFC 5696, which provides only a subset of the same capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of warning are useful: one when a link is busier than expected, and a stronger one when it is well over the limit. The earlier rules could only tell marked from unmarked. This RFC takes the code point that was left spare and uses it for the third state, so a mild warning and a severe one can be told apart.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The terms PCN-domain, PCN-node, PCN-interior-node, PCN-ingress-node, PCN-egress-node, PCN-boundary-node, PCN-traffic, PCN-packets and PCN-marking are used as defined in RFC 5559. The document adds four terms of its own.

A PCN encoding is a mapping of PCN marking states to specific codepoints in the packet header. A PCN-compatible Diffserv codepoint is a Diffserv codepoint indicating packets for which the ECN field carries PCN markings rather than the markings of RFC 3168. An operator configures PCN nodes to recognise PCN-compatible codepoints, whereas the same codepoint has no PCN-specific meaning to a node outside the PCN-domain.

A threshold-marked codepoint, abbreviated ThM, indicates a packet that has been threshold-marked, that is, marked at a PCN interior node as a result of an indication from the threshold-metering function. An excess-traffic-marked codepoint, abbreviated ETM, indicates packets marked at a PCN interior node as a result of an indication from the excess-traffic-metering function. A not-marked codepoint, abbreviated NM, indicates PCN packets that are not PCN-marked, and a not-PCN codepoint indicates packets that are not PCN-packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The naming follows one pattern: a codepoint says what has happened to a packet. NM means nothing has happened yet, ThM means the link is busier than its threshold, ETM means the link is over its limit, and 00 means the packet is not taking part in this scheme at all.

sections.title: Definition of the 3-in-1 Encoding
sections.content:
The 3-in-1 PCN encoding supports networks that need three PCN marking states encoded within the IP header, as well as those that need only two. A PCN node is configured to recognise certain Diffserv codepoints as PCN-compatible. In the encoding, a PCN-compatible codepoint combined with the four values of the ECN field gives four results: 00 means not-PCN, 10 means NM, 01 means ThM and 11 means ETM.

Inside the PCN-domain, any packet carrying a PCN-compatible codepoint whose ECN field is anything other than 00 is a PCN packet. PCN nodes MUST interpret the ECN field of a PCN packet using the 3-in-1 PCN encoding rather than RFC 3168. This does not change the behaviour for any packet with a codepoint that is not PCN-compatible, or for any node outside a PCN-domain; in all such cases the 3-in-1 encoding is not applicable and the node interprets the ECN field using RFC 3168 by default.

The four meanings are: not-PCN, which indicates a packet that uses a PCN-compatible codepoint but is not subject to PCN metering and marking; NM, which indicates a PCN packet that has not yet been marked by any PCN marker; ThM, which indicates a PCN packet marked by a threshold-marker; and ETM, which indicates a PCN packet marked by an excess-traffic-marker.
sections.plainLanguage: The two congestion bits that would normally say whether a packet saw congestion are reused here to say how badly the link was loaded when the packet passed. The traffic class code beside them says whether those bits mean anything at all.

sections.title: Requirements and Applicability
sections.content:
In accordance with the PCN architecture, PCN ingress nodes control packets entering a PCN-domain. Packets belonging to PCN-controlled flows are subject to metering and marking, and the ingress node marks them as not-marked, which is called PCN-colouring. All nodes in the domain perform metering and mark PCN packets if needed. Some edge behaviours require only a Single Marking behaviour, others require both. Where both are used, three marking states are needed: NM, ThM and ETM. Threshold-marking and excess-traffic-marking are configured to start marking at different load conditions, so one marking indicates more severe pre-congestion than the other. A fourth marking state indicating a packet marked by both markers is therefore not needed, but a fourth codepoint is needed for packets that use a PCN-compatible codepoint without taking part in PCN marking.

In all current PCN edge behaviours that use two marking behaviours, excess-traffic-marking is configured with a larger reference rate than threshold-marking, and the document takes this as a rule, defining excess-traffic-marked as the more severe mark.

Tunnelling imposes a requirement. RFC 6040 defines rules for the encapsulation and decapsulation of ECN markings within IP-in-IP tunnels, and its publication removed the tunnelling constraints that existed when the encoding of RFC 5696 was written. A problem remains if there are any legacy decapsulating tunnel endpoints within a PCN-domain: if a PCN node threshold-marks the outer header of a tunnelled packet whose inner header carries a not-marked codepoint, a legacy decapsulator forwards the packet as not-marked and the threshold-marking is lost. The applicability rules are designed to avoid this.

The encoding is applicable where two marking behaviours are used in the domain. It can also be used with only one marking behaviour, in which case one of the codepoints MUST NOT be used anywhere in the domain. With one exception, any tunnel endpoints within the domain MUST comply with the RFC 6040 encapsulation and decapsulation rules. Operators may not be able to upgrade every pre-RFC6040 tunnel endpoint; in that case a limited version of the encoding can be used, but only under a stringent condition: if any pre-RFC6040 tunnel decapsulator exists in the domain, then every PCN node in the domain MUST be configured never to set the ThM codepoint, and interior nodes MUST solely use the excess-traffic-marking function. In all other situations where legacy tunnel decapsulators might be present, the encoding is not applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: Old tunnel equipment cannot carry the milder warning, so the encoding is only safe when the network has been upgraded, or when the network uses only the stronger warning. The RFC states both conditions precisely.

sections.title: Behaviour of PCN Nodes
sections.content:
Any tunnel endpoint implementation on a PCN node MUST comply with RFC 6040, which is considered reasonable because PCN is a new capability.

At each logical ingress link, the PCN ingress node applies four functions in order: PCN-classify, PCN-police, PCN-colour and PCN-rate-meter. Classification determines whether each packet matches the filter specification of an admitted flow; packets that match are PCN packets. If ECN and PCN coexist, a packet classified as a PCN packet that arrives with the ECN field set to anything other than Not-ECT MUST pass through one of several preparatory steps before the policing and colouring steps, the choice depending on local policy. The recommended policy is to encapsulate ECN-capable PCN packets across the domain, either within another IP header using an RFC 6040 tunnel or within a lower-layer protocol capable of being PCN-marked such as MPLS, with IP-in-IP tunnelling as the default. If encapsulation is not possible, the ingress node can let ECN-capable packets through without encapsulation but MUST drop CE-marked packets at this stage, because without encapsulation there is no mechanism to propagate the CE markings across the domain and congestion collapse could result. This policy is NOT RECOMMENDED because there is no tunnel to protect the end-to-end ECN capability. Dropping the packet is also NOT RECOMMENDED.

Packet-level PCN policing prevents packets that are not PCN packets from being forwarded into the domain where interior nodes would mistake them for PCN packets. A non-PCN packet is confused with a PCN packet if it is not classified as a PCN packet, already carries a PCN-compatible codepoint, and its ECN field carries a codepoint other than Not-ECT. The ingress node MUST police such packets by re-marking the codepoint to one that is not PCN-compatible, tunnelling the packet with a codepoint in the outer header that is not PCN-compatible, or dropping the packet, which is NOT RECOMMENDED. Absent operator-specific configuration, an implementation SHOULD re-mark the codepoint to zero by default. Whichever action is chosen, the node SHOULD log the event and MAY raise an alarm, and alarms SHOULD be rate-limited so that anomalous packets do not amplify into a flood of alarm messages.

For colouring, the ingress node MUST set a PCN-compatible codepoint on all PCN packets, choosing codepoints that are already defined for use with admission-controlled traffic in order to conserve them, and MUST set the PCN codepoint of all PCN packets to not-marked.

Interior nodes have rules about what they must never do: they MUST NOT change not-PCN to any other codepoint, MUST NOT change NM to not-PCN, MUST NOT change ThM to NM or not-PCN, and MUST NOT change ETM to any other codepoint. When the threshold-meter indicates a need to mark a packet, the node MUST change NM to ThM. When the excess-traffic-meter indicates a need to mark a packet, the node MUST change NM to ETM and MUST change ThM to ETM, and where both meters indicate a need, the excess-traffic rules take precedence. Where a domain uses only one marking behaviour, the other meter SHOULD be disabled and MUST NOT trigger any marking, the node SHOULD raise a management alarm if it receives a packet carrying the other mark, and the frequency of such alarms SHOULD be limited.

The PCN egress node SHOULD set the not-PCN codepoint on all packets it forwards out of the domain. The only exception is where it is certain that revealing other codepoints will not contravene the guidance of RFC 4774, for instance when the ingress node has said explicitly that the flow is ECN-capable, though such schemes are currently only tentative ideas. If the domain is configured to use only excess-traffic-marking, the egress node MUST treat ThM as ETM, and if only threshold-marking is used it SHOULD treat ETM as ThM, raising a management alarm in either case because it means there is a misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node has a fixed part in the scheme. The entry point decides which packets are taking part and marks them as not yet marked. The middle of the network may add the warnings, and may only ever make a warning more severe. The exit point wipes the markings so that they do not confuse the network on the other side.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
BCP 124, RFC 4774, gives guidelines for specifying alternative semantics for the ECN field, sets out a number of factors to be taken into consideration and suggests techniques for the coexistence of default ECN and alternative ECN semantics. The encoding specified here uses one of those techniques: it defines PCN-compatible Diffserv codepoints as no longer supporting the default ECN semantics within a PCN-domain, so the document is compatible with BCP 124.

There is not enough space in one IP header for the 3-in-1 encoding to support both ECN marking end-to-end and PCN marking within a PCN-domain. The non-normative Appendix B discusses possible ways to do this, for example by carrying end-to-end ECN across a PCN-domain within the inner header of an IP-in-IP tunnel. The normative text in Section 5.1 requires one of these methods to be configured at the ingress node and recommends that implementations offer tunnelling as the default.

In any PCN deployment, traffic can only enter the domain through ingress nodes and leave through egress nodes. Ingress nodes ensure that any packet entering the domain has the ECN field of its outermost IP header set to the appropriate codepoint, and egress nodes then guarantee that the ECN field of any packet leaving the domain has appropriate ECN semantics. This prevents unintended leakage of ECN marks into or out of the domain and thus reduces backward-compatibility issues.

Because the PCN encoding has passed through an obsoleted earlier stage, misconfiguration mistakes may be more likely, so extra monitoring may be needed to detect and diagnose problems. An informational example is that in a controlled-load edge-behaviour scenario it could be worth the egress node detecting the onset of excess-traffic marking without any prior threshold-marking, because that might indicate an interior node wrongly configured to mark only ETM, which would have been correct for the single-marking edge behaviour. A PCN node implemented to use the obsoleted encoding of RFC 5696 could conceivably have been configured so that the threshold-meter marked what is now defined as the ETM codepoint, but there is no known deployment of that unlikely variant and no reason to believe such an implementation would ever have been built, so it seems safe to ignore the issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the same two bits do different things inside and outside the domain, the marks are cleared at the boundary. That also means the domain cannot carry the ordinary congestion signal at the same time, unless the traffic is tunnelled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PCN marking only carries a meaning within the confines of a PCN-domain. This encoding document is intended to stand independently of the architecture used to determine how specific packets are authorised to be PCN-marked, which is described in separate documents on boundary-node behaviour.

The document assumes the PCN-domain to be entirely under the control of a single operator, or a set of operators who trust each other. Future extensions to PCN might include inter-domain versions where trust cannot be assumed between domains; if such schemes are proposed, they must ensure that they can operate securely despite the lack of trust, though such considerations are beyond the scope of this document.

One potential security concern is the injection of spurious PCN marks into the domain. These can only enter if a PCN ingress node is misconfigured. The precise impact depends on which boundary-node behaviour is used, but in general spurious marks lead to admitting fewer flows into the domain, or potentially terminating too many flows. In either case good management should be able to spot the problem quickly, since the overall utilisation of the domain will rapidly fall.
sections.plainLanguage: The marks mean nothing outside the network that sets them, and they assume one operator runs the whole domain. The one risk is a misconfigured entry point letting unmarked traffic in with a warning already set, which would make the network admit less traffic than it should.
